utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All the accused are present, presentation today we are a full house. Mr. Nikolic is back. Otherwise, it's the same composition as yesterday. Mr. Haynes, good morning to you and good morning, Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours, good morning everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We're on the home straight, Mr. Pandurevic. Just taking us back a little bit, remind us where you were on the 14th of July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Zepa, in the Zepa area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And according to your understanding now, where was Dragan Obrenovic on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was partially in the field, that is to say, around Snagovo and Crni Vrh, that general area and that he spent time in the barracks from time to time, and I think that on the evening of the 14th, as he said, he was in the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about somebody else whose name hasn't come up so far in your evidence. A man called Dragan Jevtic, where was he, to your understanding, on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, he was engaged with part of the soldiers from the engineer's company in ambushes along Snagovo and Crni Vrh.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how long did he remain there, to your understanding?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was there up until the 17th, to the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And at the moment he's just a name. I'm sure people know who he is, but can you tell us what function he filled in the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander, komandir of the engineer company, of soldiers with no military training, with no rank, but as -- by profession he was a civil engineer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what did that mean that he did on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the komandir of the engineer's company and he performed that job daily, which means he was in command of the company in the spirit of his own authority and responsibility, and in the spirit of orders from his superior officers, the Chief of Staff and the chief of the engineers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. And where was he based?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire company was based north of the barracks, some 500 metres away within what was called the youth settlement which were sheds that were used to accommodate the youths and volunteers who worked on the construction of the railway line running from Zvornik to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what did he do on a day-to-day basis?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The engineer's company had assignments from -- they placed mines and obstacles of various kinds to ensure maneuvers and the movement of units which meant to build roads and maintain roads as well as bridges and also fortification work, which meant seeing to fire positions for artillery pieces and various things of that kind. And those were the kinds of tasks he did, build shelters and so on. Now, the other ways in which he commanded was that he was directly linked to daily orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to that in just a minute. But when he wasn't there, for example, between the 14th and 17th of July, who fulfilled his function?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the company command there was the deputy commander, or his title might have been assistant for morale, and that was Bogicevic. Whether his first name was Slavko, I'm not quite sure. And he was in command then also.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well let's look at P297, please, the first page, that's 134 in the B/C/S and page 14 in the English. Now, Mr. Pandurevic, what is the handwritten document that we see on the screen there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an example of a daily order for the 14th of July, 1995, by the company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And who is it apparently signed by?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The daily report should be signed by company commanders. I can't see the bottom of the page here, but I think that it was signed by Jevtic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how were daily orders given?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that in conformity with the rules of service, the company commander would issue a daily order every day and the contents of that daily order relates to the following day which means that if a daily order is issued today, for the 12th of February, its entire contents and activities relate to the next day, that is to say, the 13th of February. Now, in those orders, duty is assigned as well as guard duty, fire guards, the training of the company, and certain other tasks which might crop up outside these basic tasks. So the daily order is read out in the morning when the company is lined up, and if there are any alterations in the daily tasks and assignment, then an additional daily report or an addendum to the daily report is written. Here we can see that in the engineer's company, the order was written every day, not a day in advance as the rules of service provide. And there are no additions to the daily order, it's not supplemented. So that was probably necessary for the period that we're discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So that I'm sure that I understand you, should this document be written out before it is read out?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The company clerk entering today's date writes the order and that order has a date and a title, and nothing more. It says: Daily report of the company commander for the 12th of February, 2009, for instance. And then in point one, it says: The duty officer of the company of the 13th of February, 2009, will be Marko Markovic, Joe Blow, for example. So after writing it, it is read out in the morning when the company is lined up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. So on the face of it at least, this is what was read out to the engineering company on the 14th of July or that's what should have happened?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably. The number of soldiers who happened to be in the company at that time, this was probably read out to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we go forward one page in the document, please, to the 15th of July, page 135 in the B/C/S and page 15 in the English. And again, can we look at the foot of the page in the B/C/S so that General Pandurevic can tell us who apparently has signed that document.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was signed by Mr. Dragan Jevtic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can we go forward again another page to page 136 in the B/C/S, page 16 in the English. And again to the bottom of the page so that General Pandurevic can tell us who signed the document. Can we just -- no, other way. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was signed by Jevtic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And lastly page 137 and page 17 in English, one page further again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Also Jevtic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Given your understanding as to his whereabouts, what comments do you have to make about the fact that he appears to have signed those orders on the 14th, 15th, 16th, and 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He must have signed these signatures subsequently when he returned to the company. Somebody probably brought those orders, put them on the table, and he signed them retroactively, all of them, because during those days, he was at ambushes around Snagovo and Crni Vrh.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have a look at 7D260, please. The English is now up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's probably obvious from the title of this document, but what is it, General Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a collective report for 1995 of the engineers showing how many soldiers there were in the engineer's company, the replenishment of the company, how many officers, how many soldiers, then information about mines and explosives, vehicles, machines, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we go to the second page, please, and paragraph 8. Generally, what does paragraph 8 describe?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 8 enumerates the different material supplies divided up according to the type and source of those supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Sub-paragraph A, army stock. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each unit in the army has what we call a material formation, which means the equipment and materiel that the company uses in carrying out its assignments. And part of that material and equipment is owned by the army itself. And in peacetime, these pieces are manufactured for the army and the army has its store warehouses and depots, and it is the army who owns the technical material and that's 8 A, the army stock, and that's what the engineer's unit had as its own materiel and technical equipment, owned by the company itself. Then B, we have the inventory stock, as it says, and since the army wasn't rich enough, especially the army in this war and the JNA as well, then part of the technical equipment and materiel was taken over from certain companies and commercial enterprises so that during the war for the requirements of those units this materiel was requisitioned or mobilised, and they were placed temporarily at the disposal of the army units. And that's what is meant by the inventory stock. And C we have war booty and that is what is seized from the enemy during the war and then used for combat subsequently and that's under C, war booty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm just interested briefly in one item under sub-paragraph B and that's the BGH700 excavator. Who owned that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the -- that excavator was owned by a public enterprise called Zvornik Putevi or Zvornik roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just so we understand, did that company have use of it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the situation was very specific. Frequently, these items on the inventory stock at the disposal of the engineer's unit were then given back to companies to use when they needed to carry out their own assignments and tasks depending on the urgency and on a need-to-use basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I just want to move on to another document. Can we look at P302, please. This is a form of document we've seen a number of. It relates to a ULT 220 backhoe excavator and it says in the English, "Construction machine owned by Birac holdings," and its driver is apparently somebody called Veljko Kovacevic. Was that a machine which the Zvornik Brigade owned?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Zvornik Brigade did not own that machine either in the inventory stock or in the army stock.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Veljko Kovacevic, who is he?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Veljko Kovacevic, according to this vehicle work log, was the driver, or, rather, he handled the machine and probably someone employed in the Birac Holding Enterprise. And according to what I know, a control of the list of soldiers of the engineer's unit, in July he wasn't on the list of engineer unit soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could just, I'm sure there will be no disagreement, but there's a translation error. This is not a backhoe, this particular machine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether that's a translation issue or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know why. I wouldn't know either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Or an expert evidence issue, but it doesn't matter. I can clear that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This is the sort of machine, isn't it, that would be useful for digging holes in the ground.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what this machine looks like. It's a machine with wheels, with a cabin, and in front, it has a hoe, a big hoe, a metal hoe which is best suited for loading up material or sand or earth or whatever else. It is not suited to digging except where the ground is soft.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, we'll come on to this generic topic in a little more detail in a few minutes, but given that this machine was not owned by the Zvornik Brigade, was not part of its inventory stock, can you explain how it comes to be that there is -- a vehicle work log has been opened for it on the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This work log shows that this machine received fuel for the first time on the 15th of July, and I believe that was the first day of its usage which you can see on the next page showing when and where this machine was used. This log was probably opened on the 15th when this machine arrived and was put to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did Dragan Jevtic or his deputy have any right to give orders in relation to this driver or this machine?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they couldn't have engaged this particular piece of machinery.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you know who did?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, from Obrenovic's statement and what was told him by Jokic, the machines commandeered from companies, including Birac Holding Company, the Josanica quarry, et cetera, were requisitioned by a group of people, including Mr. Beara, on the 14th and members of the Birac Brigade. I don't know how this whole operation was conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you mention the Birac Brigade in your last answer?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said Birac Holding Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And where is that situated?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a large company in Karakaj about a kilometre north of the command, maybe less. It was working on processes alumina and aluminium, and they had this [as interpreted] type of machines that were used for reloading clay in the process of production.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now while we're discussing vehicles and fuel and the like can we have a look, please, at P377, that's the earlier duty operations officers' notebook. And if Ms. Stewart can provide you briefly with the hard copy, you will need to look at page 766, the rest of us will have a look at page 148. Now, we've looked at this before, Mr. Pandurevic, but it's the second of the entries on that page at 1400 hours. "At 1400 hours, Popovic requested a bus with a tank -- sorry requested a bus with a full tank and 500 litres of D2. Duty officer and Golic informed." I'm sure you've told us this before but just remind us who Golic is?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can only see the family name of Golic. I used to know Mr. Pavle Golic who was an intelligence officer at the Drina Corps staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can you confirm the date of this entry in the duty officers' notebook?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just remind us, I'm sure we all know, but what you were doing and what was going on at 1400 hours on the 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was precisely the time when the column of the 28th Division was either setting off or already on the way to abandon the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were you notified of this request?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, it's likely that we can, as it were, give some more detail to this note.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If we look at P1189 A in the English and C in the B/C/S, which is under seal. And in the B/C/S, we'll need to go to page 2, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, this record of a conversation between the duty officer at Palma who would have made the note we just looked at and the duty officer at Zlatar, which we now know is the corps command is recorded as being at 1358, which is two minutes before the note we just read. So it would look, wouldn't it, as though the note in the duty officers' notebook is a note of this conversation; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, logically this note would follow the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And reading this note, what is the duty officer at Palma doing, what's he asking for?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, he is acting as a person who is a dispatcher, that is to say, passing on information among various individuals working at the corps command but are posted at different locations and cannot establish direct contact amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I mean just help us. If one was, for example, at Pilica and you wanted to get in touch with corps command at Vlasenica, how would you do that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were probably a number of technical solutions for that. If someone from Pilica has a PTT number available and knows the counter PTT number in Vlasenica, he can establish direct contact. If he doesn't know the PTT number in Vlasenica, he can call the switchboard at the Zvornik Brigade staff and ask them to reconnect them or to call the duty officer at the Zvornik Brigade and ask him to establish a one-to-one contact with the duty officer at Zlatar, and that is actually the name of the person mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Let's concentrate on a couple of aspects of this conversation. B, who is Basevic - and you've told us who he was earlier in your testimony - says in the penultimate response of the first page: "Well, fuck him, don't you have 500 litres of oil? They're asking for two tonnes loaded." Would the Zvornik Brigade have had 500 litres of diesel in its stock?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it had even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And then the Palma duty officer says: "Well, I don't know. He just called me from the field and told me to pass you the message over there." How does that help us interpret the entry in the duty officers' notebook we've just looked at?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply the duty officer at Palma is the one who relayed the information, and he doesn't want to know what the problem is about, nor is he looking for a way to solve it. He quite simply left it to the people who are in charge of finding a solution. He neither has the will nor the authority to resolve these issues, as you can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to have a look at three documents now very quickly, and I think we've seen them largely before but quickly P291, please. The title of this document in English is "A Material List for Dispatch." It's dated the 16th of July, and it relates to the provision of 500 litres of fuel on the order of Captain Sreten Milosevic to the command of the Drina Corps. The addressee is Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic. And apparently, according to this document, 140 litres were subsequently returned. What is this?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This material list is a special kind of document that must always accompany the movement of materiel or fuel when it's being distributed to various units. I wouldn't like to go into too many details, but I will say that there are five copies of this list for each type of materiel, the first one is white, the second one was blue, and the last three are red. In this particular instance, the Zvornik Brigade, at the request of the chief of the technical service of the Drina Corps who was normally the one to supply the Zvornik Brigade with fuel, oil, asks the Zvornik Brigade to hand over 500 litres of fuel to the Drina Corps. In order for the Zvornik Brigade to properly deregister this fuel and that it's -- and to confirm that it's no longer in its possession and that they hold no responsibility for it any longer, this list has been issued and the responsibility was shifted to the Drina Corps for these 500 litres, or to be more precise, 360 litres because the quantity was later changed. This fuel was at the disposal of the Drina Corps and they used it for their own needs. It wasn't used by the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You've been sitting there for two and a half years, where did this 500 litres of fuel come from before it arrived at the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly. The Drina Corps command and its chief of the technical service knew exactly the sources of supply for the brigade. It might have been some of the logistics bases. Most often we were supplied with these items from the logistics base, 35th logistics base in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And who was in control of that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Zvornik Command Brigade would list their requirements for fuel, send the request to the corps command and the corps command, through the logistics organ and based on the logistics support plan, either meets the requirement of the Zvornik Brigade or doesn't meet their requirement. The person who was in charge at Drina Corps for fuel was Mr. Basevic, chief of the technical service; whereas, in the Zvornik Brigade, this was supposed also to be done by the chief of the technical service who at the time was Mr. Krstic. However, in practice, fuel was handled by Mr. Pantic, head of the traffic service, because that was his remit during peacetime as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now leaving this to one side for a moment, is it unusual for arrangements to be made between units for fuel to be provided between them?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not uncommon. Mr. Basevic could have asked the Zvornik Brigade to hand over 200 litres of fuel to the Birac Brigade or Bratunac Brigade, and the same list would have to be filled out for dispatch in order to relieve the Zvornik Brigade of this obligation vis-a-vis fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So far as you were aware was there any prior arrangement on the 16th of July that the Zvornik Brigade should provide the Drina Corps with any fuel?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I knew nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in reality, who was providing this 500 litres of fuel to Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This activity of delivering and supplying fuel was probably organized by Mr. Pantic, but I have no direct information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What does the phrase "two tonnes loaded" mean?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably there was an earlier request of the Zvornik Brigade to receive fuel which was quite an ordinary request, and Mr. Basevic probably referred to the two tonnes of fuel that he had been sent into the Zvornik Brigade through the regular procedure. However, looking through this list, I couldn't find any confirmation that two tonnes of fuel had reached the Zvornik Brigade during that period. There might be a document to that effect but I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we'll leave that now. If we take, for example, the school at Petkovci during the summer of 1995, was that used as an educational establishment?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the schools were used as educational establishments during academic year. I can't tell you for each individual school how many students they had. There was an old school in Petkovci, and I don't remember precisely which of the two schools had students and had classes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The middle of July, would that have been an academic term or would it have been school holidays?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's always school break in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Who were owned, governed, and was responsible for the school buildings in the Zvornik municipality?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that this was state property, whether owned by the municipality of Zvornik or some other municipal organ. These schools were managed by an executive committee through school principals or people in charge of education within the municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were those buildings under your lawful control as commander of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not under my control. I certainly was the brigade commander but I was not a school principal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what responsibility did you have for criminal acts that were committed in those school buildings?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no responsibility whatsoever with regard to any crime if committed by someone who was not a member of the Zvornik Brigade and outside the facilities under the jurisdiction of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What military responsibility did you have in relation to those school buildings or any of them?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each brigade has as its principal task to carry out combat operations, whether defence operations or offence operations. In other words, the main task of the Zvornik Brigade was to defend the territory and the population from attacks by enemy forces. In that sense, we provided protection and defence for the population in the entire zone including the facilities situated there. If it had happened that an enemy or a column of the 28th Division was to head towards Zvornik, our duty was to fight them in the town and try to push them outside of the town. That does not mean that automatically, we become responsible and we take ownership of the facilities where combat operations were conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were there, for example, houses in the village where your forward command post was situated?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there, but also along the entire defence line, some couple hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did people live in them?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what responsibility did you have for them?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only to protect them, to prevent the enemy from entering their houses and causing harm and damage, but I didn't interfere. I didn't go into their houses because I didn't have authority to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What right or power did you have as a brigade commander to use or requisition other people's property?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there is a need for the brigade command or any of the units to start using a facility owned by the local community or some other state organ, then the procedure for that is clearly defined, allowing the army to take possession of these facilities for temporary use. This procedure is prescribed by the minister of defence and it relates to mobilisation of people, materiel, and buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what was the procedure?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this has been discussed extensively during this trial. At the beginning of the war, I must say that there were some mistakes and wrong moves, but the procedure became very clear in 1995. Brigade commands through their organs for mobilisation, organisation, and personnel would send a request to the corps command while, on the other hand, the corps command would reformulate it and pass it on to the Ministry of Defence and its organ in charge. Depending on the decision of the ministry, it either takes action or doesn't take action. If it takes action, then mobilisation of the people and the materiel takes place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We'll just look at one example to illustrate a point, please. Can we have a look at P2900. This is a fairly notorious piece of mobilisation, this relates to the buses. And we see under the order of the minister of defence of the 12th of July, "Mobilise immediately all buses except articulated ones." Could the whole procedure be enacted pretty quickly?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a different type of example compared to what I was saying earlier on. Here, we have a direct order from the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska, that is to say, the highest organ in charge of conducting a mobilisation, and it's them issuing a direct order to the Ministry of Defence departments to carry out mobilisation. And this could have come on the heels of a decision by the Ministry of Defence itself of Republika Srpska with respect to the needs that arose or on the basis of some request and that request can be sent by the -- to the Ministry of Defence from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you request the mobilisation of any of the schools we've heard about in this case?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The schools which were used in July for accommodating prisoners of war and detaining them were not mobilised by the Zvornik Brigade nor was a request sent. During the war, there were similar requests, and some houses, privately-owned houses, were mobilised and used during the war and there are records of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to switch on to a last topic, please. When you arrived at the Zvornik Brigade in December of 1992, you've told us that Dragan Obrenovic was already there as Chief of Staff. Did you know then how long he had already been in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, I didn't know him before. I didn't know of his existence at all. And when I arrived on the 18th of December in Zvornik, 1992, that is, that's when I met him for the first time. It was a general state of confusion, so I didn't quite understand whether he was the Chief of Staff and Lieutenant-Colonel Bosancic standing in for the brigade commander or vice versa. But anyway, Obrenovic was somebody from whom I received the first information about the situation and structure of the Zvornik Brigade, and I knew that he spent time in the area during 1992, whether March or February or maybe later on as well, and that he left the area and returned to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Over the course of the next three years, he was your colleague. What were your views as to his capabilities as a soldier and a Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I very soon became convinced that Dragan Obrenovic was a typical officer of the Yugoslav People's Army. He was brought up and trained that way, and as somebody who was from -- also somebody who was from a traditional conservative family and environment. He was highly disciplined, responsible, and did his best to carry out his tasks and do his duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was he connected within the local community?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at any rate, he knew the local community far better than I did, but the greatest problem was the fact that both of us were people from outside, as they used to say, from elsewhere, not from the Zvornik municipality. But I did know that he had good relations and contacts with the president of the municipality, the mayor, and some other people, and that there were proposals on their part that he should be the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: To this day, how many conversations have you had with him about the events of the summer of 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say before that, that Obrenovic was an individual who does not easily engage in conversation and makes contacts outside his professional domain. He's not gregarious, he doesn't like to talk too much, so the two of us did not have a highly-developed friendly relations in the sense of visiting each other privately or having our families visit each other. Our relations were highly proper and correct on a professional basis, very frank and open, and I always thought that Obrenovic informed me professionally and in the proper manner about his work and what he was doing. Now, with respect to the events that we're discussing at this trial, we talked for the first time about that on the 16th in the afternoon and then on the 17th in the morning, on the 18th as well in the morning, on the 23rd, I think in the afternoon, that was, and I think I had another talk or meeting with him after his first or second interview which he gave to the OTP, but I'm not quite sure about that, whether it was his first interview or his second interview, which means five times if I've counted correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you remember what year that last conversation was and where it took place?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That last conversation was in Belgrade. I think it was 1999 and we have the interview and it says there, I might be wrong, but I think that he was in Belgrade at the time for some health problems that he had and that he went to the Medical Military Academy there and that the meeting, our meeting came about in the presence of Mr. Jevdjevic [Realtime transcript read in error "Jevcevic"], Milenko Jevdjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what did you discuss at this meeting in 1999?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we leave aside the niceties one usually said, I heard from him that he had talked to the Prosecution and I asked him what they had discussed, and he recounted the meeting and said that he had told them what he knew in July 1995 and also what I knew and what he conveyed to me, and he said that those talks were held in a proper manner. And I asked him whether he concluded from the interview that there was the possibility of him being treated as a suspect and he said no, he was there in the role of a witness and that he didn't gain the impression that he was treated as a suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything in this meeting that was new?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing new, perhaps the order in which he recounted things might have been different, but the substance of what he said was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you hear that he had been arrested when he was arrested?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that he had been arrested. I think that was sometime in May, whether it was 2000 or 2001, I can't be sure. And as far as I knew, there was no public indictment raised and that his arrest was sudden and that he was transferred to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What was your reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was surprised in view of the fact that all the information I had and all my discussions with him, especially after the interview he had given, but I don't have the knowledge that I know today. I don't have the information that I've gained during these proceedings in this trial. Whether there were reasons for the indictment or not, that's something I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just before it disappears, the name appears at the end of this -- at the top of this page "Jevcevic," probably Jevdjevic who appeared as a Defence witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jevdjevic. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Since it's been raised, were you aware of what relationship those two men had, Obrenovic and Jevdjevic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they were school friends, whether they were neighbours as well I don't know, but they knew each other better than Dragan Obrenovic and I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, as we know from history subsequent to his arrest, Dragan Obrenovic appeared before this Tribunal as an accused and entered a plea or pleas of guilty to certain charges that he faced on an indictment. What was your reaction to that when you learned of that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very shocking and a big surprise to me, and I couldn't understand why he had done that, why he did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Why do you say you couldn't understand why he had done that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everything that he told me during all our meetings and that period of time, I was not able to conclude or to know that somewhere in his soul or deep down in himself he had some knowledge and that there was something else that he didn't tell me about or that he felt guilty about something. But anyway, it was a surprise as far as I was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: General Pandurevic, I want just to return to a question that you were asked by Judge Kwon a few days ago, and I'm going to put it to you slightly differently. On the 9th of July of 1995 when your units withdrew from Zivkovo Brdo having taken that feature, how did you envisage events unfolding thereafter?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I considered that the object of the operation Krivaja 95 had been fully executed and that all the forces who had taken part in that operation had reached strong features in the topographical and military sense, that all communication had been cut off between the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa, and that what would be necessary was that the forces of the Bratunac Brigade from the Skelani Battalion should take control and positions up around those new positions and hold them, keep control of them. And that all the forces who had come from outside, including my own tactical group, that they should be returned back to base.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What changed all that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very appearance of General Mladic at the forward command post of the Drina Corps and his order that they should continue in the direction of Srebrenica changed the course of the operation itself and expanded its goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I've concluded my examination in chief of you, and I think that is pretty much precisely 30 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you've concluded it three minutes before the break schedule, so we'll have the break now after which Mr. Zivanovic, you will start your -- is there a -- yes, Mr. Bourgon, you are going to start?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yeah, I will be the first one to go, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you have changed your estimate from 4 hours to 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. I will do everything I can to try and shorten that from 12 hours, but at the present time I had to count on 12 hours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So we'll have a 25-minute -- will 25 minutes be enough for you, Mr. Bourgon, 25 minutes' break? Or do you prefer 30, I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I'm ready to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Thank you. 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, let's start, Mr. Bourgon. I don't think you need to introduce yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Given the fact that you've been sitting here in this courtroom for almost three years now, you know who I am. However, for the record allow me to introduce myself this morning. My name is Stephane Bourgon and I'm accompanied today to start this cross-examination by my colleague Jelena Nikolic, and my colleague Marie-Claude Fournier. And of course you know, Mr. Pandurevic, that we represent Drago Nikolic in these proceedings. Before I begin my cross-examination, I'd just like to come back to something you just mentioned a few moments ago when you finished your examination in chief, and this has to do with your knowledge of Dragan Obrenovic as an officer. And you stated, and that was at today page 19, lines 18 to 23, that Dragan Obrenovic, you considered to be a typical officer of the Yugoslav National Army, brought up and trained that way, highly disciplined, and responsible. My question to begin with is: Do you, Mr. Pandurevic, consider yourself at the time and even today a typical officer of the JNA brought up and trained that way?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Obrenovic and myself, just like all the other officers of the Yugoslav People's Army, were trained and brought up in the same way and prepared to take up our duties in the same way, and that was based on the policies of the league of Communists of Yugoslavia, based on socialist self-management, based on the concept of total national defence and social self protection, and on brotherhood and unity as well. As well as the fact that we had to unconditionally execute orders. I was an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army, but I always aspired to be an officer, an officer first and foremost because an officer's code of conduct implies certain elements of conduct regardless of which army you belong to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That would be very useful for the continuation of my cross-examination. A second question that comes to mind before I begin is something you said about Dragan Obrenovic and the fact that he pled guilty, and you mentioned that this came as a surprise to you. What I would like to know is what was the surprise? Was it the fact that he pled guilty or was it what he said when he pled guilty?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So what was surprising about the fact that Dragan Obrenovic pled guilty?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the knowledge and information I had about his actions during the period treated in the indictment did not tell me that he could be an accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So it is your testimony today before I begin with my questions that the information you have highlighted for us in this -- during your examination in chief, according to what you said, Dragan Obrenovic was not guilty of any crime. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The knowledge that I had and the information that he gave me, in view of all that and in view of how the events happened, took place, I considered that he had not organised it, that he hadn't ordered it, and that he hadn't taken part in it, but I knew and was conscious of the fact that he couldn't have prevented it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll also come back to this later on during my cross-examination, but right now I'd like to begin with some general questions and even before I do so, I apologise, I have to just ask you if you remember that you and I have had the opportunity of meeting on 5 December 2005 at the United Nations Detention Unit. Do you recall our meeting, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall the meeting, but I don't remember the exact date. If it was on the 5th of December, 2005, and you have noted that down, then I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you remember that on that occasion your counsel, Mr. Sarapa, was present as well as my colleague, Jelena Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I don't know if your counsel took any notes on that occasion, but did you have a chance to discuss with your counsel what you and I discussed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that the meeting was short and I talked with my -- I discussed quite a number of things with my counsel, so I can't say specifically whether we discussed that meeting of ours and, if so, what we said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we'll spend a number of hours together, sir, and my cross-examination will be divided into a series of topics which will not follow any -- will not be addressed necessarily in a chronological order. My first topic regards your knowledge and assessment of Drago Nikolic during the period you were together in the Zvornik Brigade, and that is from January 1993, that's when Drago Nikolic arrived at the Zvornik Brigade, and until April 1996 when you left the brigade. Can you confirm that during that period you and Drago Nikolic served together in the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you can confirm that Drago Nikolic actually joined the brigade, the Zvornik Brigade, and that was initially in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he came at the beginning of 1993, I thought it was February, but if you have information and a record of it being January, then I suppose that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I don't have the document with me, but I can show it at some other time. But what I'm interested in is that at the beginning, Drago Nikolic was working as a clerk in the security organ. Is that your recollection?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that before Mr. Nikolic, the chief of security was a certain Major Milosevic who held that post for a short space of time and then left and went to Valjevo, so that I remember one day, when I was out in the field during combat operations, a man appeared, he was Drago Nikolic. He introduced himself as being the new security organ in the Zvornik Brigade. And from that time on, we worked together. I did not seek him out. I did not bring him there. I did not select him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, what I would like you to confirm is that between January and March of 1993, he was not the chief of security of the brigade but he was working in the security organ. Do you recall this period, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that he worked on security affairs, whether his status was clerk or chief, to find out that you'd have to look at the documents that can either confirm that or not. If he was a clerk, occupied the post of clerk, then he worked as assistant commander for security. He did that kind of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will show you the exact document later on, but what I'd like to know is that when he was assigned as chief of security of the Zvornik Brigade, now I suggest to you that this was in March of 1993, and that at that moment you did not raise any objections to his assignment as chief of security, whether that was with the corps commander or with the chief of security of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't object for any of the officers, nor did I choose to go to the Zvornik Brigade, nor did I choose the people who would be in the Zvornik Brigade. I had the people I worked with that I had. Some were better than others. And I'm sure other people thought -- some of them thought I was good, others might have thought I was bad. So I didn't ask anybody to either withdraw Drago from the post or to leave him where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you can confirm that at the time Drago Nikolic joined the Zvornik Brigade and became the chief of security, that his rank was that of second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that he was a non-commissioned officer in the JNA, whether he had the rank of the sergeant first class, I'm not sure, but when he came to the Zvornik Brigade, I think that he had the rank of the second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to have in e-court, please, 3D542. Mr. Pandurevic, this is the book you published in 1999 called the "Sociology of the Army," and if I can have page 2 in English and page 4 in B/C/S. Do you recall, sir, you have this page in front of you that -- that's the wrong document, I apologise. It should be 3D542, please. I apologise, I have the wrong number. I'll give you the right number. 3D549.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall participating or publishing this book, sir, in 1999 called "The Sociology of the Army"?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the author of this book. I think that it was published by the faculty in Pale or the university library, but you can find this information in the book itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in this book, and in the page that you have before you, you establish a distinction between three groups of officers. If we look at the paragraph that is on the page before you, that is 2.5.8.2.2. In this paragraph, you talk about a group of lower officers and a group of higher officers; is that correct? I'm informed that maybe the -- on the right side is not completely on the screen, if we can move just a bit. Thank you. Is that better, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In this paragraph, you do distinguish between the group of lower officers and the group of higher officers.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a sociological approach to the analysis of a military organisation or army as an institution primarily from the point of view of social relationships that are being established within the organisation. This division into higher and lower ranks is conditional. There are no legal provisions applicable here in the VRS. In the JNA, they were treated as junior officers and officers. Junior officers went up to the rank of major, and higher or senior officers went up from major to colonel, whereas generals represented a separate structure within the organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we can have on the right side the next page so that we can see paragraph 2.5.8.2.3. And this is where you speak about the distinct group of general officers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we can come back to the previous page that we looked at, the previous paragraph. Now, it is your view expressed in that book that those two groups of officers, that the group of lower officers includes second lieutenant, lieutenant, and captains; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but captain first class, that's what the rank was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And then the higher group of officers begins with the rank of major and it goes to lieutenant-colonels and colonels?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but let me just tell you this: Each rank within the regular organisation of an army involves certain contents, that means that the person has to have a certain level of education and also implies certain tasks that this person has to carry out. The rank per se is meaningless if you don't have anything to fill it in with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's useful, but I will take that answer and we'll go on because we will cover this a little later on. What I need to ask you at this time, looking at the paragraph 2.2, you state that between the group of higher officers and lower officers, that there are differences. And these differences are based on noticeable social characteristics. And you also say that officers from the lower group occupy work positions of a lower level to which a lower amount of power is attached. We're not talking about Drago Nikolic for now, we're just simply talking in general. Is that the views you expressed in that book?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what is written and I still maintain this view, because there is a relation between the level of education, the rank, and the function, and this has been stipulated by the law. A second lieutenant cannot command a brigade if he hadn't graduated from the academy. The usual procedure, however, stipulates that there should be a clear link between the level of training and qualifications and the task and the rank. According to the law, there is a certain span for each rank. Therefore, lower officers command lower-ranking units, they have less power, and less authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. And you will agree with me that Drago Nikolic, during the time that he served with you in the Zvornik Brigade, held the lowest rank within the group of lower officers, and as a matter of fact, the lowest possible rank for an officer in the VRS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he held the rank of an active-duty second lieutenant. There were other both active-duty and reserve second lieutenants. Drago Nikolic acquired this rank during the war, and the person who gave him that rank probably thought he deserved it. Normally, you would acquire this rank after finishing a four-year academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that's one of my next questions, you know that Drago Nikolic never attended the military academy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, even though Drago Nikolic had the rank of second lieutenant, he was nonetheless assistant commander for security within a brigade.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you agree that this is a position which, pursuant to the military establishment, would normally require a much higher rank?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, either a major or a lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well when we met in December 2005, you said to me exactly lieutenant-colonel, but I suggest to you that the normal rank according to the establishment for the chief of security would normally be held by an officer holding the rank of major. Can you confirm this or you would have to look at the documents?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course with the rank of major, even security organs in battalions had to have a rank and that was normally captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we look at this from a seniority perspective, you will agree with me that Drago Nikolic was assigned to a position much higher than his effective rank.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that was one of the characteristics of the military profession, that you cannot choose the duty or your immediate associates or your superiors and your subordinates as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you say, sir, that this happened because of the war or could it also happen in peacetime?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about such instances in peacetime, with all due respect to Drago Nikolic, I believe that in peacetime, he would be retired as a warrant officer first class, so therefore, he would end his career as a non-commissioned officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, during your testimony, and that was at page 30781, you mentioned that Drago Nikolic was a disciplined officer. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember and I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when we met in 2005, you also mentioned disciplined, professional officer who abided at all times with regulations and orders. Do you still agree with this?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. Only I would like to add the following, that the cloak of the security service that he put on, he -- was much too big size for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, that's very useful. You also mentioned during your testimony that Drago Nikolic attended all command meetings and briefings and that his overall relationship to the commander, that is to you, was correct. Do you stand by this testimony?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Drago attended all meetings pursuant to his position, and he acted by abiding by the relationships and by the army rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can we say, therefore, that as an officer in general, you had no reason to complain regarding the demeanour of Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at this from the point of view of the rules of service and other rules that govern the relations between senior and junior officers, the subordinates and superior, there were no objections in that area. However, when it comes to carrying out his duties as per establishment, there were problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what problems were those?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said a minute ago that the cloak of the security worn by Drago Nikolic was of a much bigger size than he could have worn, and that with time, he would be swallowed by this service. He was actually very devoted to this service, and therefore believed the service much more than he believed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, let's take this step-by-step. First, I suggest to you today that you cannot recall one example where Drago Nikolic disobeyed one of your orders.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: May have in e-court please 3D233, page 3 in B/C/S and page 9 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, this is the evaluation report, personal evaluation report, which you completed and signed on 24 November 1994 concerning Drago Nikolic. Maybe we can start by the first page just to -- for the sake of allowing Mr. Pandurevic to take a look at what document we're talking about. Now, if we can go to the page I was asking for which was page 9 in English and page 3 in B/C/S. And I'd like to draw your attention, sir, to section 7 -- I'm sorry, it's 6 in English. Do you see, sir, in section 7 that you rated Drago Nikolic's performance as exceptional?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that, only I cannot see to which particular period of time this assessment refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, if we go back to the first page, you see that the period goes from the 10th of January, 1989 -- sorry, 10th of June -- I apologies, if we can go back to in B/C/S the first page of the document. 10 June 1989 until 10 June 1993. Now that's only six months that Drago had joined the brigade by that time. However, if we move to the page where you signed, that is page 3 in B/C/S, we see that this report was completed on the 24th of November, 1994. If we can move to page 3 in B/C/S, section 7 again. Do you recognise your signature? It says Vinko Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my question is although the period of this report ended in June 1993, the report was signed in 1994 in November. My question is just by that time, did you still agree with this evaluation, or did you want to change it at that time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, during the war, official appraisals were drafted very late. Each professional officer should be given an official appraisal for a period of four years which is a regular assessment. There should be some interim assessments for a variety of reasons. This is a professional appraisal of Drago Nikolic, staff sergeant first class, desk officer for security with the Zvornik Brigade. In the Army of Yugoslavia he had this same rank and was therefore supposed to be posted to this duty. The period that this refers to is the six months that he spent at the Zvornik Brigade. However, that was not the reason for me not to be able to grasp his quality and his performance, but, nevertheless, I had to consult with the commander of his former unit and with the superior security organ. And this appraisal spelled promotion for Drago Nikolic, both in the Yugoslav Army and in terms of his rank of the staff sergeant first class, and he did actually the job of a major or a --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter would kindly ask the witness to repeat the last part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Pandurevic, the interpreters didn't catch the last part of your answer. If you could repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. So this evaluation that I put down, I agree with it for the most part even to this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Of course your answer is useful but that's just what I wanted to ask you. Before looking at the review of this report by the next level, what I wanted to know was your opinion, whether by November of 1994, you saw any reason that Drago Nikolic's performance after the end of the reporting period 10 June 1993 and 11 November 1994, whether it had changed or it was also or still exceptional?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's already been said that I didn't have a full insight into the performance of Drago Nikolic with relation to all the jobs that he did and all the areas of his engagement. When I started noticing that apart from the tasks given to him by me, he is engaged in other businesses that I knew nothing about, that is when I started asking me [as interpreted] and demanding that he report to me about what he was doing and that is when the problem started.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the climax of the problems came about in late 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So is that before or after you signed this report on 11 November 1994?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I want to be a principled man, then I would say that the period to which this official appraisal refers to does not include the period of our discord. I may have though written it before the instruction that followed, and it was passed on to Drago at the time specified herein.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. We can go at length over this but that was meant to be a non-contentious part of my cross-examination, but if you want to make one then that's not a problem. By November 1994, had the problems begun between you and Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These problems had been existing on and off even in the period before that. I cannot recall all of them, but I do remember, for example, when the issue of the use of motor vehicles, we had problems. On other occasions, nobody knew where -- his whereabouts and things similar to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll move on to the next page of this report. If we can have in B/C/S page 4, and in English, page 8 -- 7, sorry. Sorry, page 6 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you see on this page, comments of the reviewing officer. First of all, can you tell by looking at this who the reviewing officer was?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here Colonel Tomic. I think his first name was Mile and he was a chief of security at the Drina Corps command, and he endorsed my appraisal and agreed with it and it was better, so I wouldn't have been happy if he didn't agree with my appraisal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We can do away with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have one last question concerning this document. You recognise that in November of 1994, you signed a document rating Drago Nikolic's performance as exceptional, and you recognise that the reviewing officer did the same, yet right now you say that you did not know of Drago's whereabouts during that period. I fail to understand. Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't put it that way exactly. I said that there were times during the day, during working hours, that Drago was engaged elsewhere without anyone at the command knowing where he was or what he was doing. None of the other officers acted like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We'll move on to the next document. If I can have in e-court document number 3D232. Sir, this is the performance evaluation report for Drago Nikolic which was signed by Lieutenant-Colonel Obrenovic on 10 June 1997. So if we look at the first page of this report, we see that it covers the period from 10 June 1993 until 10 June 1997. Do you see this, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we go on the second page of this document, where we have -- in English it would be also on the third page in English, where we have a conclusion. Now, it says here in this section: Descriptive grade and conclusion that Drago Nikolic is conscientious, that he takes initiative, and that he is a very responsible senior officer, that he is trained for independent work in the security organ, good expertise and moral qualities, his organisational capacities are very good, and he receives the grade of excellent. Can you read this in the document in your language, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you said a little earlier that when it was time for you to sign the report, the previous report which covered the period from 10 June 1989 to 10 June 1993, that you had to consult with the previous supervisors of Drago Nikolic; do you recall saying this?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I take it that Lieutenant-Colonel Obrenovic in 1997 did the same in that he consulted you before completing this report. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't consult me and he made an observation here where he says capacity -- trained for independent work in the security organ, which a commander -- which brigade commander Obrenovic would not have put there because his work in the security organ contains 80 per cent of the work that should be assessed by his superior security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We'll have plenty of opportunity, sir, to discuss the 80 per cent issue during my cross-examination. But right now, it is your testimony that Lieutenant-Colonel Obrenovic did not consult you when he gave Drago Nikolic an excellent evaluation report for the period going from 10 June 1993 to 10 June 1997. Is that what your testimony is today?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my question to you is do you agree with this evaluation even though Obrenovic did not consult you as he should have done?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What is in this report that does not correspond or that you did not agree with during the reporting period of 1993 to 1997?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't be able to make these assessments as to independent work in security organs, when he said "trained for independent work in the security organs," I don't know what Obrenovic meant by that. Secondly, with all due respect for the effort that Drago Nikolic put in, without having completed the military academy, and without having the necessary experience in the security organ, it was difficult for him to achieve that. That was what he aspired to but he was not able to fulfill it as somebody who had all the necessary education, training, courses, and rank would and that is why they stress conscientiousness and responsible work and that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now if we look at for those areas of his work of which you were informed during that period from 1993 until you left the brigade, would you agree that his performance was excellent as rated by Lieutenant-Colonel Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the tasks that I assigned him and that he executed on the basis of the orders I had given, then I would agree with the assessment made by Obrenovic -- made here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come back to those tasks that you had the opportunity of assessing in Drago Nikolic's work. I have one more question in relation to the professionalism of Drago Nikolic as your chief of security. Would you agree in general, sir, that the issue of volunteers from whatever origin who show up to fight with the Zvornik Brigade is important in that such volunteers must be carefully screened before they are accepted within the ranks of the brigade. Would you agree with this statement?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, and I didn't like to see volunteers among my ranks, especially not those with a very doubtful past.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, you lead into my next question. For example, it is very important to check whether these volunteers have a criminal background. Is that one of the things that we would have to check?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all depends of the way in which these volunteers appear in the units of the Army of Republika Srpska, how they were coming in, but at all events, you would have to look at their goals, why they had come, their characteristics, and their past. That should be checked out. And that is one of the tasks that Drago Nikolic had.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So checking their past and their goals would include, for example, whether they have a criminal background.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you were to appraise everything, everything concerning those people, then this would include everything including that criminal background. Now, whether once a criminal always a criminal holds true, I don't know. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me that if volunteers coming to join your brigade are not properly screened, that they can actually be a threat to your brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those people have their own interests, their own reasons why they came, and you know that you don't go visiting people uninvited, let alone go to war. So people coming in as volunteers to take part in a war without wishing to be subjected to military rules and regulations but chooses his time and place for going to war, that is the -- those people are the greatest impediment and obstacle to control and command of soldiers and units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you mentioned a little earlier that it was the task of Drago Nikolic to screen these volunteers. Would you agree with me that he performed this task in a very professional manner and that he indeed considered this to be a very serious task?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember one group of volunteers, it was a larger group that came to Zvornik, and I know that Drago was directly involved into the screening them and returning them to Serbia. Now, whether there were individual cases of the screening of others, I don't remember but that was certainly one of his tasks. And when we're talking about this large group that turned up, he acquitted himself affably in carrying out that task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, this group is exactly what I wanted to ask you about. Do you remember that they came from Valjevo in Serbia. Is that something you recall?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were from Uzicka Pozega which is western Serbia, not very near to Valjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you say that Drago Nikolic acquitted himself affably in carrying out that task, does that mean that he did a good job in screening them and making sure that they would not be accepted and that they were actually be sent back?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can characterise it as the regular performance of his duties and assignments, and it was his conclusion that those men did not have honourable intentions for coming, and they demonstrated that very quickly, and he was quite right when he required that they be sent back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, whether this was part of his regular duties or not, as a brigade commander, were you satisfied to see that you would not be faced with the -- having to deal with a large group of individuals not having, as you say, honourable intentions. Were you satisfied that this work had been done?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I was always satisfied when the people who worked with me did their job properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But my question is much more specific. I'm not talking about people doing their job properly. I'm talking specifically of this group of people who were turned back because they did not have, as you say, honourable intentions. Were you satisfied to see that for this specific example, that's one -- that this was one less problem for you as the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said I was satisfied. And it was the task of my associates and the people that worked with me to see that I have as few problems as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you remember individuals by the name of Slovenac, Niski and Profa? Do these names ring a bell to you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
